item.title: Selective hunting may be making Madagascar’s largest bats smaller, study says
item.description: Madagascar’s largest fruit bat is getting smaller, and hunting may be partly to blame, a recent study suggests. The Malagasy flying fox (Pteropus rufus) feeds mainly on fruit and nectar, making it an important pollinator and seed disperser. But the species is also hunted for meat, both for subsistence and commercial sale. Hunting is legal […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: South West Water’s failure to fix leaks ‘putting customer supplies at risk’
item.description: With parts of region served by company in severe drought still, regulators give it six weeks to come up with action plan Repeated failures by South West Water to tackle leaks are putting customers at higher risks of losing water supplies as parts of the region remain in severe drought, regulators have said. In a warning to the privatised company that serves 1.8 million people across the south-west of England, the regulators said it had been failing to meet targets to reduce leaks and repair burst pipes for seven years. Continue reading... Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: ‘No one cares about the little guy’: Sri Lanka’s fishers still reeling from 2021 toxic plastic spill
item.description: A stricken container ship shed tonnes of tiny pellets called nurdles on the west coast. Five years on, locals are counting the cost to marine life and livelihoods On the beach in Pamunugama, on Sri Lanka’s west coast, women in uniform work under the scorching sun. They sift through rubbish washed ashore, searching among the usual litter for something much smaller: tiny plastic pellets. Five years ago, in May 2021, this same beach was swamped with pellets as smoke rose over the Indian Ocean. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report
item.description: Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050 Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study. Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: World’s wettest rainstorms are getting wetter, affecting flood and drought risk
item.description: Events that deliver about half of global rainfall are getting shorter but more intense, with wide-ranging implications The world’s wettest rainstorms produce about half of the global annual rainfall. Now a study shows that these intense downpours have become shorter in duration and fewer in number, compressing the same amount of rain into quicker and more extreme events, with implications for flood and drought risk. Chiyuan Miao and colleagues from Beijing Normal University in China analysed daily measurements between 1980 and 2022 from more than 19,000 rain gauges around the world. They… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: El papa León XIV visitará Zaña, el pueblo marcado por la tragedia en Perú
item.description: Durante siglos, Zaña, en el norte de Perú, ha estado rodeada de relatos sobre tragedias y una supuesta maldición desde que una devastadora inundación destruyó gran parte de la ciudad colonial en el siglo XVIII. Hoy, este pueblo de unos 4.000 habitantes se prepara para un acontecimiento histórico: la visita del papa al santuario de Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo. Los vecinos han impulsado colectas y trabajos de restauración para recibir al pontífice. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Mitigating the ecological consequences of light pollution
item.description: Light pollution is one of the fastest-growing and least-regulated environmental changes worldwide. It disrupts biological processes at all levels—from genes to entire ecosystems—and contributes significantly to global biodiversity loss. A recent review article, in which the Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) participated, addresses the ecological consequences of artificial nighttime lighting. Based on a comprehensive assessment of the impacts on organisms on land and in water, the authors identify priorities for research and management. The Review Article was… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trained dogs detected invasive plant species in Germany with 75% accuracy
item.description: Invasive alien species (IAS) are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide. A study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth at Helmholtz-Centre for Environmental Research—UFZ, Germany, and colleagues found that with training, volunteer dog-handler teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Ministers urged to go further than proposed cut to 110 decibels to ease acute stress on birds and others animals Campaigners are calling on the UK government to protect the welfare of wild animals by cutting the maximum noise level of fireworks sold to the public from 120 to 90 decibels. item.description: Researchers find the birds’ guano feeds algal blooms that absorb significantly more solar energy Penguin poo is making the Antarctic snow melt faster, a study shows. As temperatures rise, penguins are waddling closer to the south pole, with potential for this previously unrecognised phenomenon to affect a wider area. Snow algae are tiny single-celled plants that make a home in some of the coldest places on Earth. When nutrients are scarce, the algae produces red pigments to protect itself from the sun and slow growth. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Cooking is a bigger source of harmful air particles than vehicle exhausts in London and Beijing

item.description: What does a healthy river look like? For most of us, an obvious answer would involve two aspects: water flowing through a channel and green vegetation along its banks.
